title: Multi-scale reconstruction of single-ion damage tracks in diamond via nitrogen-vacancy centers
authors: Daniel G. Ang, Jiashen Tang, Maximilian Shen, Michael Titze, Gavishta Liyanage, Jordan Chapman, Chinmay Bharathulwar, Andrew T. Gilpin, Tanguy Terlier, Edward S. Bielejec, Vsevolod Ivanov, Ronald L. Walsworth
abstract: Understanding particle-induced damage tracks in solid-state materials underpins emerging applications in rare-event detection and quantum defect engineering. Resolving these tracks requires multi-scale readout, from event localization at the millimeter scale to track-morphology reconstruction at the nanoscale. Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond provide such a platform, combining optical localization with quantum sensing of track morphology. Here, we implant sub-MeV carbon ions into nitrogen-rich diamond and detect individual recoil events via spatially localized NV formation. We develop a simulation framework that explains the observed NV yield and predicts that directional information is retained in the NV distribution after annealing. Machine learning further recovers much of the information lost to defect diffusion and limited NV yield, improving head-tail classification to a level comparable to pre-annealed vacancy tracks. Measurements of NV spin coherence indicate compatibility with nanoscale track reconstruction via NV strain mapping and magnetic gradient-based techniques. These results identify promising pathways toward NV-diamond directional detectors for rare events, while the track-modeling framework has broader implications for paleodetection and quantum material synthesis.
summary: This work develops a multi-scale framework to reconstruct directional information from single-ion damage tracks within diamond using Nitrogen-Vacancy centers. By coupling ion implantation simulations with defect diffusion modeling and applying Machine Learning classification, the authors demonstrate a robust method for detecting rare events crucial for dark matter searches.
main_problem: The study aims to reconstruct single-ion damage tracks formed by particle recoils in diamond, which is crucial for developing next-generation rare-event detectors.
main_result: A combined framework using advanced simulation (KMC) and Machine Learning significantly improves the classification of track directionality after annealing, achieving high efficiency comparable to pre-annealing conditions.
method: The research combines experimental characterization using NV photoluminescence mapping with computational modeling involving Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations for defect diffusion and Machine Learning inference for pattern recognition.
model_or_system: The physical system is diamond crystal lattice containing Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) color centers. The model involves simulating the creation of vacancies/interstitials from ion implantation, followed by annealing dynamics governed by defect diffusion kinetics.
key_observables: NV yield per implanted ion ($	ext{NNV}$), track asymmetry metric ($A$), and ML posterior probability ($P$) used for directional classification.
important_parameters: Sub-MeV carbon ion energy, annealing temperature ($800^\circ	ext{C}$), false positive rate ($	ext{FPR} \lesssim 5\%$), and spatial scales from $\mu	ext{m}$ to $	ext{nm}$.
main_assumptions: The KMC simulations assume specific reaction pathways (e.g., first-nearest neighbor interactions) which are refined by DFT calculations; the ML approach assumes sufficient feature space coverage for accurate inference.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate PL maps showing localized NV ensembles, histograms comparing simulated vs. measured $	ext{NNV}$ yields, and cumulative plots comparing classification performance between traditional metrics and Machine Learning approaches.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical necessity of multi-scale readout to detailing simulation pipelines (SIIMPL/KMC), quantifying defect evolution, developing ML classifiers for directionality, and finally confirming quantum sensing compatibility via spin coherence measurements.
why_interesting: It bridges solid-state physics defects with advanced data science techniques (ML) to solve a complex physical measurement problem, which is highly relevant for understanding disorder effects in quantum materials.
